exhibits.title: Scientific Societies

when.display: Accademia dei Lincei 1603; Royal Society 1660; Académie des sciences 1666

exhibits.change: Societies where claims were demonstrated, witnessed, debated and published.
exhibits.context: The Royal Society's Philosophical Transactions (1665) was one of the first scientific journals. Members replicated experiments and corresponded across Europe.
exhibits.significance: Peer scrutiny and publication — the social machinery of modern science.

exhibits.title: The Newspaper
exhibits.change: News printed on a regular schedule for anyone who could pay.
exhibits.context: Johann Carolus's 'Relation' is often considered the first newspaper. Earlier, handwritten newsletters and government gazettes (such as China's dibao) circulated among officials.
exhibits.significance: Regular public information — the beginning of the press and public opinion.

exhibits.title: The Telescope
exhibits.change: Two lenses in a tube: moons around Jupiter, mountains on the Moon.
exhibits.context: Hans Lipperhey applied for a patent in 1608. Galileo improved the instrument and published Sidereus Nuncius (1610), describing Jupiter's moons, lunar mountains and countless stars.
exhibits.significance: Observation beyond human senses — decisive evidence against an Earth-centred cosmos.

exhibits.title: Kepler's Laws
exhibits.change: Planets move in ellipses, sweeping equal areas in equal times.
exhibits.context: Working from Tycho Brahe's data, Johannes Kepler published his first two laws in Astronomia Nova (1609) and the third in Harmonices Mundi (1619).
exhibits.significance: Exact mathematical laws of the heavens — the target Newton's gravity would explain.

exhibits.title: The Microscope

when.display: compound microscopes by the 1620s; microbes observed in 1676

exhibits.change: A hidden world: cells, sperm, blood corpuscles and 'animalcules'.
exhibits.context: Robert Hooke's Micrographia (1665) named 'cells'. Antonie van Leeuwenhoek's powerful single-lens microscopes revealed bacteria and protists, reported to the Royal Society in 1676.
exhibits.significance: Opened the microbial world that germ theory and modern biology would explain.

exhibits.title: The Circulation of Blood

regions.note: Ibn al-Nafis described pulmonary circulation in the 13th century.

exhibits.change: The heart pumps blood around a closed circuit.
exhibits.context: William Harvey's De Motu Cordis used measurement and experiment to show that blood circulates. Ibn al-Nafis had described the pulmonary circuit in 13th-century Damascus and Cairo.
exhibits.significance: Physiology by quantitative experiment.

exhibits.title: The Weight of Air
exhibits.change: A column of mercury showed the atmosphere pressing down — and a vacuum above it.
exhibits.context: Evangelista Torricelli's experiment produced the first sustained vacuum and the barometer. Pascal showed pressure falls with altitude; Guericke's air pump followed.
exhibits.significance: Atmospheric pressure made steam engines, weather science and vacuum technology thinkable.

exhibits.title: The Pendulum Clock
exhibits.change: A swinging pendulum cut clock error from minutes to seconds a day.
exhibits.context: Christiaan Huygens built the first pendulum clock, applying Galileo's observation of pendulum regularity.
exhibits.significance: Precise time for science — the most accurate timekeeper for nearly three centuries.

exhibits.title: The Scientific Revolution
exhibits.change: Knowledge of nature came to rest on experiment, measurement, mathematics and open publication.
exhibits.context: Between Copernicus and Newton, European scholars built on Greek, Islamic, Indian and Chinese foundations and on new instruments to overturn inherited authorities. Experimental method, mathematical laws and scientific societies with journals formed a self-correcting system of inquiry.
exhibits.significance: It created the method that produced most of the exhibits in the galleries beyond this one.

uncertainty.note: Historians debate whether it was a sudden 'revolution', how uniquely European it was, and how much it depended on earlier traditions.

exhibits.title: Calculus

regions.note: Leibniz, working in Paris and Hanover.
The Kerala school had infinite series for trigonometric functions centuries earlier.

exhibits.change: Mathematics of change: rates, slopes, areas and motion.
exhibits.context: Isaac Newton and Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz developed calculus independently; a bitter priority dispute followed. Leibniz's notation is the one still used. Mathematicians of the Kerala school had earlier derived infinite series related to calculus.
exhibits.significance: The language of physics and engineering.

exhibits.title: Seki's Determinants
exhibits.change: Determinants discovered in Japan a decade before Europe.
exhibits.context: Seki Takakazu, working within the Japanese wasan tradition, described determinants for solving systems of equations in 1683; Leibniz arrived at them independently in 1693.
exhibits.significance: A clear case of parallel mathematical discovery.

exhibits.title: Newton's Principia
exhibits.change: One set of laws for a falling apple and an orbiting Moon.
exhibits.context: The Principia set out three laws of motion and universal gravitation, deriving Kepler's laws and explaining tides and comet orbits.
exhibits.significance: The first unified mathematical physics; the framework of engineering until the 20th century.

exhibits.title: Iron Smelted with Coke
exhibits.change: Coal, baked into coke, replaced scarce charcoal in the blast furnace.
exhibits.context: Abraham Darby's use of coke freed iron production from forests. His grandson's Iron Bridge (1779) displayed cast iron as a structural material.
exhibits.significance: Cheap iron on an industrial scale, fuelled by fossil carbon.

exhibits.title: Newcomen's Engine
exhibits.change: Condensing steam made a vacuum; the atmosphere pushed a piston and pumped a mine.
exhibits.context: Thomas Newcomen's atmospheric engine drained coal mines for decades. It was inefficient but reliable; Savery's earlier pump (1698) had worked poorly.
exhibits.significance: The first practical machine to turn heat into sustained mechanical work.

exhibits.title: Jantar Mantar
exhibits.change: Instruments the size of buildings measured the sky.
exhibits.context: Maharaja Jai Singh II built masonry observatories in five cities; the Jaipur sundial is among the largest in the world. He also compiled astronomical tables drawing on Persian and European work.
exhibits.significance: A late flowering of the observatory tradition in South Asia.

exhibits.title: The Flying Shuttle
exhibits.change: A shuttle knocked across the loom doubled a weaver's speed.
exhibits.context: John Kay's flying shuttle let one weaver make wide cloth quickly — creating a shortage of yarn that spurred inventions in spinning.
exhibits.significance: One bottleneck solved created another — the chain reaction of textile mechanisation.

exhibits.title: The Marine Chronometer
exhibits.change: A clock that kept time at sea gave ships their longitude.
exhibits.context: John Harrison spent decades on sea clocks; his H4 watch lost only seconds on a voyage to Jamaica. Longitude could then be found by comparing local noon with home-port time.
exhibits.significance: Safe, accurate ocean navigation — and a triumph of precision engineering.

exhibits.title: Naming Life
exhibits.change: Every species given a two-part name in a nested hierarchy.
exhibits.context: Carl Linnaeus's system gave naturalists worldwide a shared vocabulary. Many of the specimens and names came from Indigenous knowledge gathered by travelling students.
exhibits.significance: A universal catalogue of life, later reinterpreted as a family tree.

exhibits.title: The Encyclopédie
exhibits.change: Twenty-eight volumes gathering the arts, trades and sciences for public use.
exhibits.context: Edited by Diderot and d'Alembert, with detailed plates of workshops and machines, it spread Enlightenment ideas and practical technical knowledge.
exhibits.significance: An ancestor of every modern reference work, including those online.

exhibits.title: Lightning Is Electricity
exhibits.change: Sparks in a jar and the bolt from the sky were shown to be the same force.
exhibits.context: Following Benjamin Franklin's proposals, experimenters in France drew electricity from storm clouds. The lightning rod followed.
exhibits.significance: Electricity became a natural force to be studied, not a parlour curiosity.
